rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient and a strong final solvent to locate the elution window while minimizing truncation risk. The midpoint temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction once critical pairs are identified.

Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to probe selectivity in the crowded middle cluster. The current last peak is comfortably within 10 minutes, so resolving the critical pairs is the priority.

Use a shallower gradient at the best temperature so far to improve the remaining critical separation. There is ample time margin below 10 minutes, while further heating risks compressing the neighboring pair that already narrowed at 50 C.

Increase temperature by one step to improve selectivity for the persistent critical pair. Retain the 14-minute gradient because it provided more separation for neighboring peaks and kept the last peak below 10 minutes.
The maximum CRF is achieved; now shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep temperature fixed and check whether both marginal pairs remain above R = 1.5.

Reduce the gradient span to restore most of injection 4’s shallower slope while retaining the shorter programmed gradient. This should recover the newly limiting separation and may keep all pairs resolved with slightly earlier final elution.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 6’s slope to test whether a stronger starting solvent shortens elution without sacrificing critical separations. Injection 6 remains the fastest fully resolved method established so far.

The higher starting organic fraction hurt the limiting separation, so test a lower start combined with a steeper, shorter gradient. This may preserve the middle-cluster resolution while bringing the last peak out earlier than injection 6.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 8 to recover the marginal separation while keeping its low starting organic fraction. This targets full resolution with a last peak earlier than the 8.00-minute benchmark, while checking the other near-threshold pair.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a substantially faster gradient at the highest temperature for an alternative selectivity window. The middle peaks may change elution order, so this is an exploratory run rather than an assumed improvement.

Probe the low-temperature selectivity window using the original scouting gradient. This tests whether a different elution order can provide full resolution faster than the established 7.60-minute method.

Test a stronger starting solvent at 60 C to explore separation on the opposite side of the middle-cluster elution-order crossover. The longer gradient than injection 10 may improve the other crowded separation while still giving rapid final elution.

Lower the starting organic fraction to recover early-pair retention, while steepening the gradient to explore the balance between the two middle-cluster separations. This tests a nearby fast-method candidate without repeating a previous gradient.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 40 C opens a different selectivity window for the middle cluster. This isolates the slope effect against injection 1 and the temperature effect against injection 10, while targeting much faster elution.

Test whether a stronger starting solvent at 50 C improves the persistent middle-cluster separation while retaining adequate spacing for the earliest peaks. This explores a faster alternative, with injection 9 preserved as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test an intermediate temperature in the fast-gradient region, where 60 C improved one middle separation but compressed another. This run checks whether 55 C balances those competing separations while maintaining adequate retention of the earliest peaks.

Refine near the confirmed fully resolved methods with a slope between injections 5 and 6. This targets a shorter elution time than injection 6 and potentially more balanced resolution margins than injection 9.

Preserve injection 9’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending the programmed gradient two minutes earlier. Since the outlet gradient ends at 8.65 minutes, after its 7.60-minute last peak, the successful separation should be retained.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 17 to locate the full-resolution boundary at a 0.10 starting fraction. This should shorten final elution, although the limiting middle pair may fall just below R = 1.5.

Test a shallower gradient with the higher starting fraction to improve both critical-pair margins while aiming to keep the last peak below 10 minutes. The maximum score is already secured; this run seeks a less marginal fully resolved method.

Test a cooler selectivity window with a moderately shallower gradient than the 40 C scouting run. Cooling may separate the middle pair on the opposite side of its crossover, while the longer gradient helps protect neighboring separations.

Return to the successful 55 C region and slightly reduce the slope from injection 20 to recover its single marginal pair. This targets full resolution with improved critical-pair margins while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test one final faster candidate using a lower starting fraction to protect the middle separation that deteriorated with stronger starts. At 50 C, the steeper gradient may improve the other critical pair; injection 18 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Slightly steepen injection 22’s gradient to shorten its elution time while retaining its improved resolution margins. This refines the more robust maximum-score alternative; injection 18 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Preserve the starting composition, temperature, and slope of the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, while extending the gradient to a stronger final solvent. This should retain its 7.60-minute last peak and maximum CRF while providing a stronger post-separation wash.
